en: Preface to the Recorded Sayings of Chan Master Wujiandu of Tiantai:
In the direct lineage of the Zen school, one speaks only of authenticity and not of concealment or manifestation.

Those who have truly attained the Eye of the True Dharma and constantly act as teachers to humans and devas, though they may bury their traces and erase their shadows, their refined radiance will naturally burst forth through a thousand years. Like jade, they remain lustrous; like mountains, they remain steadfast.
Its brilliance causes the river to shimmer with the beauty of hidden pearls; protected by divine beings, it cannot be buried or lost.

When Bodhidharma came from the West, the lineage split into five branches at the time of the Sixth Patriarch Caoxi. The direct transmission of the Linji school split into two branches at the time of Wuzu Fayan.
Duanqiao Lun and Xueyan Qin were like two eagles striking together or two steeds galloping side by side.

Later on, one would soar while the other gathered, one would leap while the other remained hidden; all within the inconceivable realm of great capacity and great function, they upheld the life-force of the Buddhas and Patriarchs.
How could this have been achieved through the ostentatious display of fame or by contending with the gateways of worldly dharmas?—Wu Jian.
Master Du was the true bone and marrow descendant of Duanqiao; Master Jin Jie’an, however, was a "lion cub" of the thirteenth generation after Wujian.
This record has spanned exactly three hundred years from the Dingyou year of the Yuan dynasty to the present Dingyou year of the Ming.
Previously hidden in famous mountains and transmitted only among those who knew it, it has suddenly emerged...
It has been brought forth from the dragon palaces and ocean treasuries, enabling the Venerable Jinming Jie to polish it and bring it to great brilliance;

this is indeed a most extraordinary and wondrous cause and condition. From the Great Master Zhizhe of Tiantai down to the eminent patriarchs Daji and Gaoyuan, who planted their staffs upon Mount Huading and caused their fame to resound throughout all quarters, none could match the Venerable Wujian’s ability to [manifest this] amidst such lofty and frigid heights.
In a secluded and solitary place, he spread out a single sitting mat and spent forty years of spring and autumn there, his footsteps never crossing the threshold of the door.

Yet, his reputation for the Way overflowed, drawing disciples who hurried to take refuge in him. In his pointing and lifting, his expositions, and his instructions, he manifested jeweled royal lands from within a single hair-pore and turned the Great Dharma Wheel within a speck of dust.
Speaking in accordance with the nature of reality, his spiritual sharpness was towering and steep; as he regarded the world...
As for these words and characters that fill the void of space, how could they be limited to merely a thousand or ten thousand *li*?

The record of facts and the eulogies are fully contained within the preface by the Imperial Scholar Huang Jinqing of Jinhua, the inscription for the stupa of the Great Master Tany’o of Guoqing Temple, and the colophon by Chan Master Yuansou of Shuangjing Temple;
these are sufficient as evidence for examination throughout the ages. The fourth month of the late summer, the Dingyou year of the Shunzhi era.
On the middle day of the waxing moon, composed by the Disciple of Caoxi, the Layman Li Dao-yi (styled Fuzheng),
and the Retired Vice Minister of the Court of Judicial Review and Former Second-Rank Juren of the Wuchen Year, Yu Bu-lang, at the Sǎo Ān of Tán Zhēnmò, Director of the National Academy.
Preface to the Recorded Sayings of Chan Master Wujian Du:
On Mount Huading in Tiantai there dwells a great bhikṣu named Chan Master Wujian Du. The Way of this Chan Master is that which directly inherits the orthodox transmission of Linji.
Indeed, since Bodhidharma [brought] the Mahā... (Note: The provided source text appears to be truncated. The translation reflects the available portion.)
The unsurpassed True Dharma obtained by Kāśyapa reached the Eastern Land and was directly transmitted to those of superior capacity. Subsequently, it branched into two;
while the Mind-Seal (Citta-mudrā) was transmitted alone to Caoxi, it further divided into five schools, yet the Linji lineage flourished most vigorously.
In terms of the abundance of realized disciples, none surpassed the single school of Linji. After seven transmissions, it reached Yang...

Qi Ba-yun, the Fifth Patriarch Yuanwu, was truly one who established no dharma, whose source was direct and immediate, and who led people to clarify the mind and see the nature so as to attain Buddhahood.
Among those who transmitted his lineage were Master Long of Huqiu and Master Daohui Gaofeng;

both stood out preeminently in establishing the Way of the Teachings at the beginning of the Southern Song dynasty’s relocation south of the Yangtze, serving as pillars of the Chan school in the southeastern region.
Fengcheng eventually became preeminent in his time. Long’s lineage was passed down through four generations to Ying’an Hua, Mianjie, Po’an Xian, and Wuzhun Shanfeng.
As for Shanfeng’s lineage, it included Duqiao Lun and Xueyan Qin.
During the final years of the Song dynasty, the venerable patriarchs of the school passed away one after another, and—
These two masters alone propagated the Way in the southeast, taking it as their personal responsibility to uphold and spread the school's tradition;
they may truly be called the pillars of the Chan gate. Master Lun’s lineage was passed to Fǎngshān Bǎo, and the Chan Master received the Dharma from Master Bǎo;
thus, his teaching style was rigorous and his spiritual mechanisms were swift and alert, leaving no cause for shame toward his ancestors. He resided at Huādǐng.
For forty years of cold and heat, he maintained his ascetic practices with steadfast resolve; his footprints never once descended from the mountain, nor did he rise from his seat.
Yet the weight of his reputation for the Way moved those both far and near. Is this his practice of the Way not a source of glory for the orthodox transmission of Linji?
Initially, Master Qin’s lineage was passed to Gaofeng Miao and Zhongfeng Ben; and as for Master Miao—
He sat in solemn meditation at Tianmu Mountain, establishing a "Death Barrier" to await practitioners; throughout his life, he never descended from the mountain.
He and Chan Master Shishi were like uncles and nephews within the Dharma gate, and thus their practice of the Way was as if following a single standard.
Since the founding of our present dynasty, those who have been able to cause the Linji tradition to flourish once again in the southeast are Master Ben and Chan Master [Shishi].

He was truly a master; it may be said that his legacy was magnificent. Long after the Chan Master had passed away, his disciple Daochang collected his recorded sayings with the intention of publishing them in woodblocks for circulation.
He came to request a preface from me. Regarding the subtle, profound, lofty, and remote aspects of the Master’s Way, I am indeed incapable of knowing them.
I have therefore briefly recounted the origins of its lineage and inscribed this upon the first leaf, hoping that—

If the reader can perceive the Way through direct observation, then their understanding will have surpassed half the journey. Written on the day of Jiazi in the second month of the seventeenth year of Zhizheng (the year of Dingyou),
by Huang Min, Grand Master of the Palace with Rank of Zhongfeng Daifu, former Academician of the Hanlin Academy, Director of the Office of Imperial Edicts,
Joint Editor of the National History, and Supervisor of the Imperial Lectures.

I have not seen the recorded sayings (*yulu*) of the Venerable Master Wujian; I have obtained only the remnants of what has been damaged by insects and have compiled them into two volumes for publication.

This shall enable readers not only to emulate the ancient worthies but also to further perceive the greatness of the Patriarch, who sat upon Mount Huading for forty years. His feet... [are worn smooth].

Without ever crossing the threshold [of his chamber], the fragrance of his Way spread far and wide, moving the entire world. The former ruler bestowed upon him the name Zhongqishan (Mount Ultimate Response).
Within this place, he manifested teachings in accordance with the capacities of beings, excavating the profound essence of the "Eye-opening" (Kāyadṛṣṭi) doctrine.

Fearing that I might privately retain it, I have specially set it forth to share it with the world. I trouble you, Layman, to deliver it to the *Śūraṅgama Sūtra* Hall so that it may be consulted by all.
I am most fortunate.

He addressed the assembly: "The wind blows coolly; the sun shines brightly. *Campaka* flowers bloom, filling the air with fragrance; in a single night, spring grass grows by the pond.
How pitiable and yet how laughable is Old Gautama! For forty-nine years he said nothing at all. A-he-he!
He struck his meditation seat and descended from it.
Addressing the assembly: If one discusses this matter, the Buddhas of the three periods and the entire Great Canon of teachings cannot fully explain it;

the elder monks throughout the land cannot even bring it forth for discussion. Even if you possess the power of eloquence that overturns the ocean and the spiritual mechanism that topples the mountains, not a single point of it will be of any use.
You people of noble character: when hungry, eat; when weary, sleep; when hot, seek the cool; when cold, [seek the warmth].
Thus, they sit facing the fire; each one is naturally true, each one is luminous and wondrous. How can you step forward to discuss Chan and discuss the Way?
You have mistakenly taken fish eyes for pearls and wrongly identified orange peel as fire. Have you not heard it said: "The great capacity must be thoroughly penetrating;
the great function must be direct. Not recognizing the Master Kong Qiu of the eastern house, you instead seek rites and music in a foreign land.
Holding up his staff, the Master said, "A mistake. He then raised the case of Layman Pang asking Mazu Daoshi, "Who is it that does not take the myriad dharmas as a companion?
Mazu replied, "Wait until you can drink up all the water of the West River in a single gulp; then I will tell you. The Layman attained realization.
The Master composed a verse on this: "Drinking up the waters of the West River in a single gulp— The partridge cries out amidst the deep blossoms."
[The Master] entered the hall. "Even if you were to directly accept it right now, it would still be more than ten thousand miles away from the white clouds.

He lowered his staff and descended from the seat. Small-scale Sermon: Linji, upon entering the gate, would shout; Deshan, upon entering the gate, would strike with his staff. These were heroes of a chaotic age.
When Old Xue bowed his head and returned to his hermitage, or when Magu carried a hoe into the garden, they were like traitors in a time of peace. Therefore it is said: "Within the phrase..."
Cease the mind. Within the mind, do not let phrases linger; mind and phrases are of different orders. How, then, will you understand?
Even if you were to turn your body over upon the edge of a sword or ride a horse upon the edge of jagged ice, it would still be but ripples surging without a wind.
Have you not seen Yunmen say: "Throughout the entire universe and the great earth, there is not so much as a hair’s breadth of affliction—this is still a turning phrase. Do not see even one..."
The Dharma is, for now, only half-presented; one must further know that there is the "full presentation.
But how is the full presentation? [He] strikes the whisk and says: "Since leaving the cave, I have had no rival; where I can afford to spare others, I spare them.
He then cites Linji hearing Deshan address the assembly, saying: "If you can speak it, thirty blows; if you cannot speak it, thirty blows."
"Whip! Jie ordered his attendant to go and ask: "Why do you say that whether one can speak it or not, there are thirty blows?
"If he strikes you, catch him and give him a shove; see what happens. When the attendant arrived there and posed the question as before, Deshan struck him.
The attendant caught him and gave him a shove; Deshan then returned to his quarters.
The attendant returned and reported this to Linji. Linji said, "I have always suspected this fellow.
Nevertheless, do you see Deshan? The attendant hesitated, and Linji struck him. The Master said, "A crossbow of a thousand *jin*—would it ever be triggered for a mere mouse?
To 'cross the blade on a rushing torrent' and 'pass the flame faster than the wind'—the two elders certainly possessed these qualities; yet, examine them closely."
Upon examination, these thirty blows should have been eaten by me alone. Why? Because when the head does not lead with vigor, it brings trouble upon the entire army.
(He strikes the whisk and descends from the seat.)
Small Assembly: The Tathāgatas of the past have already accomplished this gate: it is like seeking a form in a dream or grasping the moon in water.
The Bodhisattvas of the present each now enter perfect clarity: it is like catching a rat at the riverbank and smashing the oil jar.
Those who practice and study in the future should rely upon this very Dharma; since they themselves are without sores, do not wound them. Within the state beyond calculation—

It turns into calculation; within the pathless, it turns into a path. Little do they realize that the butcher’s shop and the wine tavern fully manifest the ancestral style of the Buddhas, and the bustling marketplace and red dust reveal the very core of the Patriarchs.

If one can bring forth the one to clarify the three, and discern the subtlest nuances with the eyes, how could this be anything less than ten thousand miles of white clouds? *Sha!* Flowers bloom and fall, left to the wind. By oneself—
A pure fragrance filled the heavens and the earth. Again, Xuefeng addressed the assembly, saying, "The Buddhas of the three periods turn the Great Dharma Wheel upon the flames.
Xuansha said, "Lately, the government's regulations have become somewhat strict. Xuefeng asked, "How so?
Xuansha replied, "They do not permit encroaching on others' stalls or seizing their markets. Xuefeng involuntarily stuck out his tongue. Yunmen said, "The flames are the Three [Bodies]."
"The Buddhas of the world preach the Dharma; the Buddhas of the three periods of time stand upon the ground and listen. The Master said:

"Xuefeng and his disciples thought they were propagating the Great Teaching, yet they did not realize they were merely racing about with intellectual interpretations and flaunting their learning and hearing.
Yunmen, unable to restrain his impatience, said: 'The flames preach the Dharma for the Buddhas of the three periods of time. But tell me, what Dharma do they ultimately speak?"

Baiyun Du entered for an interview and asked, “I do not yet understand the secret meaning of the West—how is it?
The Master said, “Wait until Mount Salar nods its head, and I shall tell you. Baiyun shook his hand as if to answer. The Master then gave a shout. Baiyun said, “Mount Salar...”
"Summit! White waves surge to the heavens. Flowers bloom after芒種 (Mángzhòng); leaves fall before立秋 (Lìqiū).
The Master said, "In my house, there is no leftover soup or stale rice. Wuduo said, "How can this not be leftover soup and stale rice? The Master nodded his head in approval.
The Dharma words for Inspector Xu:
Faith is the primordial mother of merit; it nurtures all roots of goodness. The ancient sages have graciously bestowed upon us these skillful means.
Every word and phrase uttered is nothing other than administering medicine according to the illness; how could it ever bind people with substantial dharmas?
When deluded, there are a thousand differences and ten thousand distinctions; when awakened, all matters are of one family.

This is because, since time immemorial, one has been shrouded by ignorance and afflictions, unable to penetrate through and see the source. How can one allow oneself to be submerged in worldly toil and vainly lose one's radiance?
If one harbors even a slight distinction within a single thought-moment, one will fall into the three evil realms; at that time, though one regrets and laments, it will be of no avail.
Those of old who were resolute in the Way dwelt in crags and caves, wearing clothes of grass and eating food from trees;

when they encountered sounds or forms, it was like planting flowers upon a stone, and when they saw fame or profit, it was as if grit had entered their eyes. Nowadays, most people are preoccupied with being clever...
Driven by sharp and clever intelligence, they study extensively and accumulate vast learning merely to provide material for their discourses.
Like silkworms spinning cocoons to entangle and bind themselves, they cannot let go of their traps and snares; this is truly pitiable.

Administrative Officer Daian is one who is devoted to this Way, casting aside fame and profit like worn-out sandals and embracing a life of austerity like a dhūta practitioner. Alas! There is no second path under heaven, and there are no two sages.
With these two minds, how can you allow yourself to be self-indulgent and self-abandoning, willingly accepting the cycle of birth and death?

You must completely let go of worldly attachments and suddenly forget the distinction between self and others. With fierce resolve and intense clarity, investigate this closely and continuously; then, naturally, you will accord with the Way.
Li Zunxu said: "To practice Chan, one must be an iron man. As soon as the hand touches the heart, one must decide: take directly toward supreme Bodhi."
Do not concern yourself with any matters of right or wrong.

Reveal to Marshal Xiao the unsurpassed, wondrous Way, which is inherently possessed by every person; it is merely that, due to the delusions and attachments accumulated since beginningless kalpas, one has been unable to realize it.
To suddenly clarify the scenery of one’s original ground, a person of great capacity must employ genuine effort:

take up an ancient *huatou* (critical phrase) and, in all places, maintain it with constant, subtle mindfulness, heart and mind without interruption. Only when you suddenly shatter the web of doubt will you first possess the portion of freedom.
If you are half-doubting and half-believing, it will be difficult to grasp it at last. It is just as Guan Yu was at the hundred... [passage continues].
It is like taking the head of Yan Liang amidst ten thousand troops; one need not fear the realm before them and can decide victory from a thousand miles away—how joyful this is!
Nowadays, scholars and gentlemen drown themselves in words and language, failing to apply genuine effort.

If you wish to penetrate thoroughly the root-source of birth and death, you must investigate according to reality and awaken according to reality; then you may be joined with the Buddhas and Patriarchs.
They walk together hand in hand. [The Master] manifests the body of a high official to preach the Dharma for them.
He showed Kuai Chaofeng that our Buddha, the World-Honored One, acts as the Great Physician-King for all sentient beings. As the Sūtra says: "I am like a skilled physician who knows..."

When a physician prescribes medicine, whether it is taken or not is not the fault of the doctor. The entire Tripitaka, comprising five thousand and forty-eight fascicles, consists entirely of medicinal prescriptions for treating the world.
One might suppose that these are medicines administered according to the illness; yet one fails to realize that the medicines are many while the illnesses are grave.
The patriarchs of later generations were unable to eliminate the source of this ailment; instead, they applied further moxa-blades upon the scars of previous burns.
Some said, "Directly pointing at the human mind, one sees one's nature and becomes a Buddha"; others said, "Mind is itself Buddha," or "Neither mind nor Buddha.

Some would shout "Ho! the moment a student hesitated; others would strike the moment a student opened their mouth. Since the capacities of those to be taught were not uniform, the remedies employed were likewise manifold.
If it is digested, it becomes *amṛta* (clarified butter); if not digested, it becomes poison. When the illness has departed but the medicine remains, this too is an illness.
Xuansha addressed the assembly, saying: "You all say you know how to engage with beings and benefit living creatures. But suppose you encounter three types of patients—how would you engage them?
To one suffering from blindness, you raise a mallet or brandish a whisk, yet he does not see. To one suffering from deafness, you speak of *samādhi*, yet he..."
Furthermore, have you not heard of the one suffering from muteness? When instructed to speak, he could not. If one cannot engage these three types of people, the Buddha-dharma lacks efficacy.
There was a monk who requested instruction from Yunmen. Yunmen said, "Prostrate yourself. As the monk rose from his prostration, Yunmen struck him with his staff.
The monk stepped back, and Yunmen asked, "Are you not blind? Yunmen then called to the monk to come closer.
[The Master] asked, "Are you not suffering from deafness? The monk said, "Do you understand? The monk said, "I do not understand.
The Master said, "Are you not suffering from dumbness? At these words, the monk attained realization. Master Yunmen was accustomed to using this medicine;
however, it could only kill people, it could not bring them back to life. Why? A superior physician regards that which is not medicine as medicine. As for a mediocre one—
Physicians take medicine as medicine; inferior physicians turn medicine into non-medicine. Now tell me: why is asafoetida without reality?
Why is mercury without falsity? Why is licorice so sweet? Why is yellow myrobalan so bitter?
If you are a discerning practitioner of the Way, do not seek realization through the sense of taste. —Master Lingtang Guishan.
You have long cultivated the studies of Confucianism and further acquired the subtle arts of Lu and Bian.

You have always harbored the intention to save all beings, and have specifically come from afar to inquire about the essentials of entering the Way, desiring to penetrate thoroughly to the very root of birth and death.
Therefore, I cite the words of the Fifth Patriarch, Master Yan: "Śākyamuni and Maitreya are still his servants. Now tell me, who is he? Simply, during the twelve periods of the day...

During this time, investigate closely and continuously. After a long period of such mastery, there will suddenly come a moment of breakthrough, like a feverish illness breaking into a sweat—how joyful that would be!

During the long summer, Layman Xu Zhigong was fortunate enough to dwell together with me among the rocks and beneath the pines; at every word and every silence, my joy was beyond measure. Now tell me:
is this the same as, or different from, the ancients who, during their summers, did not hear the two characters "Right Cause" (*zhengyin*)? I ask you, Layman Zhigong, to provide a response.

A turning word: to fix one’s eyes before the pivot of the occasion is not yet to belong to the ranks of the eminent. In the past, Chan Master Fenyang Shanzhao studied under more than seventy virtuous teachers.
Later, upon meeting Shoushan, he asked, "What is the meaning behind Baizhang rolling up the mat?
Shoushan said, "The dragon’s sleeve is swept aside, and the entire body is revealed. Fenyang then asked, "What about your own understanding, Master? Shoushan said, "Where the elephant king walks..."
The traces of the fox were severed. At this point, Fenyang attained great enlightenment. Rising from his prostrations, he said:

"The moon in the empty expanse of the ten-thousand-year-old emerald pool—only after repeated searching and grasping does one finally come to know it. A monk standing nearby asked, "What principle did you perceive that you have thus come to accept yourself?
Fenyang replied, "This is precisely where I let go of my body and surrender my life. Observe how that ancient master ultimately would not settle for himself.
A minor result. Even if you have some realization through Zen meditation, if you do not meet a true teacher, it is called "deluded Zen.
If the traces of awakening are not eliminated, they instead become a cage that restricts you in every situation; you remain seated within a realm of superior subtlety.
The predecessors called this the "falcon-scented robe," which is most difficult to cast off. You should examine this with great care; first of all, you must not fall into the darkness.
Making a living in a ghost cave at the foot of a mountain; secondly, one must not play with a ball on a rushing torrent.
Within the four modes of deportment, apply yourself with urgency; suddenly, you will break through the gateway of the face. It turns out it was simply the person of old.
There is not even a hair’s breadth of obstruction or hindrance. To say that the way is long is merely to encourage you. To the Abbot of Juekong Hermitage:

That which perceives and that which is perceived are empty; when emptiness and perception are perfectly complete, what is heard and the hearing itself are exhausted. When hearing is exhausted, one does not dwell therein. If you see it in this way, you have attained it.
Having already set out upon the journey, one has not yet seen the Way. If the mind still harbors the measure of the sage, one remains entangled in adventitious defilements (*āgantuka-kleśa*).

If one's own views have not yet been forgotten, it is no different from leakage (*sāsrava*). How can one discuss the mind or nature, or lecture on Chan and the Way, and expect this to constitute the True Dharma Vehicle?

Those of old who were resolved upon the Way did not allow fame or profit to disturb their hearts, nor did they give thought to wealth or treasures. They utterly forgot the ways of the world, wearing garments of grass.
Eating wood (living frugally), one should take the realization of reality through reality as one's goal. If it is merely water dripping from the mouth, it only increases karmic consciousness.
Examining this from the outset, what kind of matter has been accomplished? Cleverness cannot withstand birth and death; dry wisdom cannot avoid saṃsāra.
Master Yuantong was sincere in his devotion to the Way; he was truly a banner of light in the final age. However—
Your intelligence is excessive. Sitting within the realm of the sublime, you have not yet escaped from what you see and hear;
it is like the moon in water. You need a word every day as an admonition. Alas! We have met at the summit of White Cloud Mountain.
We have met within the Yuan Tong Hermitage. What more is there to betray? Do you still wish to take up a blunt brush to smear upon white paper?
To Zen practitioner Dai:
In days of yore, Xuefeng underwent many ascetic practices; he did not decline his nine arrivals and three ascents.

Suddenly turning back with a mind intent on the ancients, he rode a single staff through the spring breeze down from the green peaks. Zen practitioner Dai of Sanyan dwells together with me at the mountain summit; he is about to travel everywhere...
"San. He produced a sheet of paper and requested a verse. An ancient worthy said, "If you recognize this staff, the business of a lifetime of study is finished.
Now tell me: which of these is the staff? Which is the business of study? If you can say it, you still do not possess the eye of study.
If you cannot say it, you likewise do not possess the eye of study.
Showing that the Nun was Without Fault:
Formerly, in the assembly of Master Dahui, there was a Chan practitioner named Miaocong who had practiced with rigorous intensity since his youth.
He once spent the summer retreat at Mount Jing. One day, as Dahui ascended the hall, he cited the example of Shitou showing it to Yaoshan: "Even doing so is not permitted."
"Not so" is not permitted; "so" and "not so" are both not permitted. Miaozong attained awakening at this point.
Dahui raised the story of Yantou striking a ferryman who encountered an old woman to interrogate him. Miaozong offered this verse: "A single-leaf skiff floats upon the vast and boundless;
Paddling oars and dancing the boat-pole, one transcends the musical scales. Cloudy mountains and the sea moon are both cast aside; One wins..."
Zhuang Zhou’s dream of being a butterfly has long since passed. Behold those who have attained it: at every turn, they possess their own path for emergence;

how could they ever die beneath the words of others? The Chan practitioner Jingshan has diligently pursued the Way and traveled from afar to knock at my mountain peak, carrying paper in his sleeve to beg for words of instruction.

Furthermore, I have long hidden my拙 (awkwardness/mediocrity) deep within the clouds and have never yet uttered a single word of "no" to anyone. Moved by the urgency of his earnest request, I have complied.

Because I have written this "Miaozong" (Wondrous Totality), I have witnessed the causes and conditions for Great Wisdom (*mahāprajñā*). If one is able to investigate according to reality, one will reach the ground of great peace and bliss;
even a hundred thousand Miaozongs would then be left in the shade. I have composed a verse to encourage him: His refined bearing does not yield to the Nun of Mount Mo;
His pure and flawless nature is not yet considered extraordinary. With a single "pfft" from the ground, true joy and liberation arise— A hero indeed!
Truly a man of integrity. He showed this to Xingxin Jie Gao’an Worthy, saying:
"Your parents nourished your body; your teachers and friends fulfilled your aspirations. You were not pressed by hunger or cold."

"Without the toil of corvée labor, if you do not now apply yourself with diligence to accomplish the work of the Path, what face will you have to show your parents, teachers, and friends on another day?
These words may vie with the sun and moon for their radiance; for leaving the household life is not intended to seek leisure or pursue pleasure.
One must be able to practice what is difficult to practice, learn what is difficult to learn, endure what is difficult to endure, and relinquish what is difficult to relinquish."
In all circumstances, take up the ancient *huatou* and investigate it closely and continuously, making awakening your standard. Furthermore, you must not harbor a mind that awaits awakening;
the four debts of gratitude are difficult to repay, and the offerings of the faithful are difficult to digest. Time passes swiftly; be careful not to let it go to waste.
To the Chan practitioner Daochang:
The ancients left the home life for the true cause; they traveled on pilgrimage for the true cause.

It was because they did not understand birth and death, because they sought to sever afflictions, transcend the triple world, and continue the Buddha’s life of wisdom—not to seek ease and comfort, nor to seek warmth and fullness, nor to seek the tip of a snail's horn.

This refers to profit and fame. To distance oneself from the dust of the world and leave secular life behind, to transcend the mire, and to dwell in mountain forests and rock caves with single-minded diligence to accomplish the work of the Way—Master Xianshan Qian addressed the assembly, saying: "Conceptualization and discrimination are certainly not it.
Seeing, hearing, sensing, and knowing are certainly not it. Walking, standing, sitting, and lying down are certainly not it. Questioning, answering, and speech are certainly not it."
It is certainly not so. For now, cut off these four paths and instead bring up Zhaozhou’s “Mu” (無).
Then you will naturally be able to let out a hearty laugh; it will no longer be accompanied by empty words or superficial talk. Strive toward this!
Shizongben said to the novice Xingu:
"To raise a child, there is no need for instruction; they will naturally understand when they stumble. That which can be taught is but the dregs of speech.

The monk Hanshan, with his head covered and feet bare, bids farewell; Lüqiu, be careful not to seek after tracks.
Together with Kemi, we release the children;

the long-accumulated rain has finally ceased and the summer heat is cleared. The smoke of the imperial incense newly stains the light silk of the *ge* robe. Throughout the ten thousand worlds of the great chiliocosm, all follow the same script and laws;
the land produces worthy and virtuous men to assist the sagely brilliance.
Presented to Academician Zhao Qingshan of Nanming:

Deep in spring, we ascended Mount Huading together. We sought out the ancient cinnabar well of Ge Hong; the vastness of the six realms remains unknown to men, yet the moon pours forth the reflections of a thousand peaks and ten thousand peaks.
I tell you, Chan Master Gui, in my whole life I have laughed at myself for being utterly incapable. With a tattered robe covering my head, I dwell amidst the green peaks;
a broom grows in the corner of the wall, yet I have never picked it up to serve as a black staff.
To Zen practitioner Hai:
Beside the cliffs of Potalaka, the ocean waves are vast; by the side of the Slippery Stone Bridge, diverging paths abound.
It is said that hearing of these things is not as good as seeing them for oneself—suddenly, a solitary bird calls out from the misty vines.

I grant thirty blows to Zen student Jian of Japan before he has even stepped onto the ship’s railing. You must thoroughly investigate this sentence of immediate realization: "The Flower Peak rises forty-eight thousand fathoms;
flowing water, pines, and wind serve as the guide."
To show the Chan practitioner Xuán:
flames erupting from an icy river are not marvelous; a flower blooming on a withered tree is likewise no marvel. Sitting together at the foot of a pine tree, there is no other speech;
raising one’s eyes, one sees only white clouds drifting by.
Presented to the Astrologer Liu:
White clouds and crimson leaves surround my thatched gate; I unroll my astrological charts and sit upon the roots of the rocks. Fortune and misfortune are entirely summoned by the mind;
where there is no mind, fortune and misfortune need not be discussed.

To Anxin: What a fine method for settling the mind! Its wondrousness is manifest before one's eyes, yet it cannot be transmitted. Who would have known that the moon at the bottom of the pond is originally the sky above the roof?
To He Dafu, upon casting a bell:
Forged from within the great smelting furnace, even stubborn bronze and dull iron are all excellent materials.
As their pure sound spreads far throughout the three thousand worlds, the weary eyes of those caught in the turmoil of labor are opened wide.
To Inspector Chang of the Western Terrace:
The golden belt at your waist has already been set aside; With a diligent heart and resolute will, you have sought instruction from all quarters.
Having personally ascended to the summit of Mount Hua, The clouds are naturally leisurely, while the waters are naturally busy.
Answer: The Monk of Dongyu has swallowed the Buddhas of the three ages in a single gulp; there is no need to discuss his cold words or stale remarks.
For three coins he bought a yellow-sand bowl, which he buried by the hearth to boil vegetable roots.

Answer: Having been granted leave with great honor, the imperial favor descends like radiance from the side of the sun. His saffron robes are newly dyed by the smoke of the Imperial incense burner. How shall this old monk in the clouds repay such grace?
He offers a single stick of pure incense before the Buddha.

To show that for one who constantly practices meditation, the ordinary mind is the Way: take a step and enter the wild weeds. To know the essential meaning, there is one who is old and one who is not yet old.
[This concludes] the ritual at the stupa of Venerable Fángshān.
Cloud peaks briefly lowered as I paid homage to his compassionate countenance; his words of instruction were as if heard within a single day.
Standing before the stupa, half-submerged in mud, the lake’s light grew dim as the rain fell in mist.

National Teacher Shao received his training under the principle that "there is no dharma outside the mind," yet he exposed the family’s disgrace. With green mountains filling the eyes, the path ahead is long.
This place where he practiced the Way for over four hundred years—cedar seeds scattered from the eaves diffuse a fragrant scent.
Verses on the Dharmakāya:
A bird builds its nest at the head of a rapid torrent; sesame seeds are planted upon flat boulders. The void leaps and bounds while Mount Sumeru dances;
iron trees spontaneously blossom before the wind.
The new latrine is freshly built;
how should one use it? One must strive to discharge that one excrement.
If you merely squat there idly, you will only add foul odors to your body.

In the narrow hermitage, within the hollow of a lotus fiber, lies the vastness of heaven and earth; a mustard seed contains Mount Sumeru, and the world is wide. With fingers and fists, the functions of the mechanism differ;
the wooden gate is always closed amidst the white clouds.
The lazy ox is not without intent when plowing the stony field; the nose-rope has been snapped for many years. Reclining crosswise within the three realms, heaven and earth seem narrow;
how laughable that Liangshan could not finish his painting.
Lan’an does not yet rise even when the sun has reached the top of the three bamboo poles; when people come, he does not even raise his fist. The hundred birds carrying flowers have no news;
a single melody of pine wind pours forth through the azure stream.
Without ornate patterns, naturally sweet and simple—what else could one do? A grass mat and hempen robes are most fitting for oneself.
With not a single trace of the "original word" remaining in the breast, a single blow shatters the five Mount Sumerus.
Xinan suddenly experienced the "dropping of the bucket bottom"; he was decisively free of further doubt. Sitting alone beneath a thatched eaves, his fist met the highest pivot.
— Yuetam.
A single wheel is ever bright and pure; it cools the depths of the azure waves. Nothing can compare to it; its clear light shines through past and present.
Amidst the four modes of deportment, he walks within the mountains. Crimson thorn flowers bloom like a canopy of brocade. The secluded birds cry out. I ask you practitioners of Zen: what do you say?
I dwell in the mountains; alone, I am too weary even to prop open my thatched gate. A pair of aged birds fly here and there every day.
I sit among the mountain peaks, amidst moss-covered boulders at the roots of pines. Looking up, they must surely laugh at me for being as idle as the white clouds.
Lying in the mountains, my straw mat has long since worn out and torn apart. The cold nights are long; I roast two or three pieces of firewood.

At the hour of Pingdan (Tiger), the Song of the Twelve Hours says: "Investigate the meaning of the Patriarchs; do not be negligent. Putting on clothes and eating food are ordinary matters. [The state of] "Great Death" for one...

Only upon returning does one truly encounter intimacy; the sun rises at the hour of the Rabbit (卯). Those of worldly wisdom boast of their cleverness, yet how can they ever succeed in cooking sand into porridge?
A painted cake has never been able to satisfy hunger; practicing by grasping at appearances is nothing but bitter toil. At the hour of eating, [one must partake of the real].
While washing his face, he suddenly touched his nose; it turns out he was just the same person as before. At the hour of Youzhong (8–10 a.m.), the blue-eyed barbarian monk still remains at a loss.
Secret Master Ma holds a wooden staff in his hand; Daowu sits upon his seat, holding a ceremonial tablet and dancing.
**At noon (11:00 AM):** The great earth is gathered up, yet not an inch of soil remains. A hairless hawk soars through the heavens; a tawny-tailed tiger swallows a tiger whole.
**At mid-afternoon (12:00 PM):** The primary meaning of the West is laid bare. Mañjuśrī was not the teacher of the seven Buddhas;
how could Śākyamuni have received the prediction from Dīpaṃkara? **In the late afternoon (1:00 PM):** Though you see it with clarity, it is still not intimate.
If you enter through the gate, you must know it is not your own treasure. The sun enters the hour of You (5–7 p.m.).
Facing others, I am too weary to open my foul mouth. Mice swarm together to steal taro and chestnuts; they overturn the broken earthenware jar at the head of the bed.
At the hour of Xū (7–9 PM): Again, I see the moon rising from the mountain peak; walking alone upon the stone by the pine roots, the wind laughs as dewdrops moisten my hempen robe.

At the hour of Hài (9–11 PM): The mountain barbarian Dù Rénquán remains entirely unchanged; with a single blow of his fist, he shatters the five Mount Sumerus, and with a step of faith, he overturns the four great oceans.
At the hour of Zǐ (11 PM–1 AM): Not begrudging it for your sake, I raise it up once more.

Zhaozhou was able to employ the twelve hours, yet he was employed by the twelve hours themselves: At the hour of Chou (1–3 a.m.), when the rooster crows, the thatched eaves have not been swept and the green moss is thick.
Fluttering yellow leaves fall before the crags; Fragments of white clouds arise at the valley mouth.
Regarding the mechanism of language, I have a single word that has not been transmitted by the thousand sages. Ānanda joined his palms; Kāśyapa raised his fists.
I have a single phrase—take care not to misrepresent it: "Yesterday there was a fine wind; today there is a fine rain."
I have a single mechanism; I show it clearly to you. If you do not understand it, you will be sawn apart like a plummet.
I have a single barrier; even to understand it is most difficult. The wind howls through ten thousand ravines; snow covers ten thousand mountains.
I have a single phrase: it is neither thought nor deliberation. Brewing tea in an earthen pot, roasting taro by a clay stove—this is the mountain dweller’s poem:
"A lone pine tree, a wisp of smoke; a single orb of moonlight, a pool of spring. If one were to depict this in a painting of returning home, this would be it.
Painting: I have added a *dhūta* monk sitting by the rock.
Zhuangzi had the intention to equate all things; I too am without a mind to equate myself with things. Sitting alone upon my *bōtuán*, the spring moon is warm;
a solitary bird cries out beyond the window.
The cries of wild geese ring out clearly amidst the cold clouds; the skirt is mended, yet the trousers must be worn again. As the red sun slants westward, the shadows of the pines shift;
the rush sandals are moved to dry in the shade of the eaves.
The mountain hermitage also prepares for the coming cold; the window paper is double-glued for extra strength. Dried bamboo firewood is tied into bundles;
at nightfall, each person takes some to burn.
In a three-bay bamboo-thatched hut beneath green pines, with four walls thickly plastered, it is a fitting place to settle oneself.
Neither reading the sutras nor practicing seated meditation, the ceramic incense burner gathers dust all day long.

Passing west of the pit, I gathered wild greens among the peach blossoms; the tender grass reached my waist, and the path seemed lost. The spring rain teased out the sun, leaving the day’s light pale;
the cuckoo’s cry ceased, and the bamboo pheasant took up its song.
In the mountain hermitage, I sit in silence through the deep night; a single cold lamp flickers, half-formed into a flower. A swarm of rats steals the yams and chestnuts;
they overturn the broken earthen pot at the head of my bed.
White clouds constantly lock the peaks of a thousand mountains; standing here, one is high, and dwelling here, one is solitary. When weary from digging the earth, one sleeps a single nap;
using the hoe as a pillow is superior to coral.

Dwelling in hibernation deep within the clouds, my livelihood is sparse; let gain and loss, prosperity and decay come as they may. Clearing new fields and tilling the soil serve as my leisurely diversion;
in my Dharma-body, there is not even a trace of anything else.
The turnips are harvested and steamed until soft; dried in the sun, they are fragrant and tender, surpassing yellow rhizomes.
Having stilled the sores of hunger during both meals, who cares for the sound of sleet falling before the eaves?

Master Yongming’s diction is as lofty as his carrying of pitcher and bowl while dwelling among the green peaks. Let the world’s praise and blame rise and fall as they may; he deeply clarifies our Patriarch’s teaching of the single transmission.
In leisure, he composes unconventional poems in the style of Hanshan. Wild monkeys cry out in thirst as they peer into the mountain stream; flocks of forest birds gather to pluck [the fruit].
Frost on the branches; a hundred-tongued bird appreciates the *yangchun* melody. Through the vastness of a thousand years, there is but one Ziqi.

In the play of intellect, there is no power to gauge depth or shallowness. On the green mountains, the path remains for pursuit. Listening to the teachings, two鬓 (temples) turn white strand by strand.
All the various minds of a lifetime have been extinguished. From ancient times to now, mulberry fields have changed many times. Morning and evening, the sun and moon move of their own accord.
Rising and sinking. Long has it been since I returned from washing my bowl after the midday meal; having eaten my fill and slept in peace, I do not loosen my robe.
On returning home, one must forget the old path; yet before reaching home, the road feels far away.

Whenever I see fallen blossoms drifting with the passing waters, I smile as I watch withered trees reaching toward the heavens. The ocean of learning, though thousands of fathoms deep, is but empty waves; within this single field of the mind, [virtue] grows long.
A different sprout; he has constructed a thatched hut large enough to accommodate his knees. The empty window is unobstructed by the four surrounding mountains.
There is not even a spot to plant a needle—this is what is called being at one's limit. In his old age, dwelling in seclusion, his heart grows increasingly indolent.

Sentient perceptions are suddenly forgotten, becoming like withered wood. Form and fragrance remain undestroyed, as the visiting bees value them. The grasses and trees of the thousand mountains return to spring green. A single scroll of ancient painting.
The intent is profound. Examining the old path before the hermitage, the deer that once carried blossoms in their mouths have long left no trace.

The forests and springs are silent and desolate, making it difficult to summon companions; the worldly paths are winding and crooked, necessarily requiring a go-between. The madness of grasping at the moon and riding the whale has not yet ceased;
the ambition to soar on clouds and ride cranes must surely be broken. The light of wisdom shines from within, brightening the sky of one’s own nature; the seeds of flowers follow the mind of man.
The earth opens; his two feet sit cross-legged upon fragrant, soft grass. This body knows how many lifetimes have passed; yin reaches its limit and yang arises, yang returns to yin.
Myriad functions are never obscured across the past, future, and present. Flowers of various hues fill the world as sentient beings contemplate;
the clear moon reflects in a tranquil pool—the heart of all Buddhas. As winter ends, the cold plum flower exhales jade-like fragrance; welcoming spring, the bright willow casts its shadow.
Swinging the golden bells, there is ultimately no distinction between purity and defilement, nor any fixed location.

Birds occasionally perform their wondrous songs; every phenomenon is perfectly interfused, its subtlety beyond description. Without remainder and without lack, he is the Honored One among the multitude.

Rain nourishes the white stones, causing mica to grow; dew draws forth green moss upon the thatched gate. Boiling wood sprouts until they are soft, they possess a clear and subtle flavor; repeatedly burning cypress seeds, they are tranquil.
No words. When meeting a Zen practitioner, one simply points to Zen. The tradition of the ancient Buddhas is fortunately still preserved.
Amidst a heap of withered yellow leaves, I have purchased a mountain dwelling. Having no virtue to bestow upon others, I simply attend to myself;

it is a joy to be a guest beneath the forest trees. Let the dust accumulate on the books at my desk. The two matters of life and death return to the breath; true and false, both conditions have already—

Severing [all attachments]. On that day, Master Huiyuan cultivated pure deeds; he diligently formed a society on Mount Kuanglu. His single-minded devotion was as tranquil as the realm of white clouds;

it is truly laughable how those burdened by toil are busy every day. There are surely no elixirs for prolonging life on the islands of the sea, and the immortals' methods for transforming base metals into gold are but empty fancies.
The stars and constellations of the central heavens shine upon the cold waters, while the smoke and clouds darken the horizon as far as the eye can see.
The eight wildernesses are silent; from my solitary meditation on the humble wooden platform, a single clear strike of the stone chime awakens me to the vastness of heaven.
With pine and vines forming a canopy, the house above my head is green. Birds accustomed to landing on the altar-platform are not startled. Cloud-sheets open of their own accord and close again;
for the traveler’s heart, there is neither seeing off nor welcoming. Spring returns to the great earth and the myriad flowers grow tender; the waters rise in the stream before the mountain.
The riverbanks are level; my severing of attachments and the disfigurement of my form are now complete. Who is it that comes to involve themselves in worldly sentiments?
The *kāṣāya* robe remains unfurled, left to gather dust. For thirty years, I have ceased seeking the ford. Beyond the heavens, the thousand-mile-long thoughts are difficult to exhaust;
amidst the clouds, one’s entire life grows old. After the rain, the myriad peaks deepen their emerald hue; in the secluded valley, flowers bloom late.
Seeing Spring: A Message to Old Wang of East Village. This year’s poverty exceeds last year’s poverty.
The morning bells resonate deeply from the mountain ridges, And once again, ten thousand worldly affairs arise. Today I dwell within this mountain-water retreat;
In years past, I used to gaze upon it in paintings. Ten thousand pines and countless flowers, With the red sun three *gān* high, dews still clinging.
It has not yet dried; one need only attain this mind that is as level as the earth. Let the paths of deer and horses deceive as they will—whom can they deceive?
Who would laboriously judge the mind and consciousness? The pine roots and *fuling* fungi of ancient times: when the Way is severed, it is only then that one accords with the Way;

when there is no gratitude to repay, it is only then that one knows gratitude. For many years, the three garments have been of coarse brown cloth; in the still night, the moon shines upon the blue sky.
A single scar. A hundred billion Buddhas, as numerous as the sands of the Ganges, could not be digested by swallowing them whole in a single gulp.
When a fellow man visits me, joy fills my brows; sitting deep in the night, the moonlight is faint.

Were it not for half a lifetime of eradicating accumulated habits, how could a single word immediately strike the vital point? The lamp reveals its remaining embers as red petals fall; the fire stirs the floating ashes to reveal their white.
Snow falls. Who would be willing to speak of the solitude of the deep mountains? Tomorrow morning, you must not yet speak of returning home;

the thousand sounds of the night *bāṇa* chants continue as the moon has not yet reached its end. One knows not when the incense of the carved seal-patterns will be consumed. The broken raft drifts amidst the clamor within the stillness of the Eastern Sea;
upon one pillow, one is busy within the dream of the Southern Branch. I realize for myself that the light and shadow of this *saṃsāra* are short; I long to return to the pure peace of *Sukhāvatī*.
The head is long; jeweled banners and pearl nets provide layered protection.

Such manifold adornments are immeasurable. Three feet suffice to support this six-foot frame. As for worldly fame and profit beyond heaven, let others scheme for them. Since the thought [of self] has ceased, all conditions have subsided.
Who cares if the mountains are level or the myriad phenomena wither? Waterbirds lead their chicks along the mountain stream; woodsmen seek companions across the valley.
The forest calls out. Those with hearts must surely be like Bo Yi and Shu Qi; for a thousand ages on Mount Shouyang they became famished men.
In the clear, cold clouds, those who reach them are rare. Vastly open, things and self return to the same source. The pink peach and white plum blossom embody the True Dharma;
the warbling swallows and singing orioles reveal the wondrous mechanism. Fresh waters rise in the stream as fish shadows thicken; lingering clouds return to the cave as the sun sets.
The light is faint; Zhi repays his enlightened friend with a single silence.
Is it so? It is not that it is not so. From this point on, the worldly path shall never again turn its head. My companions, Pangsong and Hanshi, are like me.

The dark pearl is attained spontaneously without seeking; clever wisdom is but a vain exertion of effort. Exhausted they lie down, hungry they eat, passing the years and months; amidst the blossoming flowers and falling leaves, they recognize [the truth].
In the Spring and Autumn Annals, it is said: "Pitiful are those who crave profit and fame; with one mad heart, they harbor a hundred anxieties.

The gates of the Dharma are infinite, yet I feel shame for my lack of accomplishment. The jade hare and golden crow wane and wax again and again. Facing every object, I constantly dissolve delusive thoughts;

possessing this body, day by day I grow weary of this floating life. Amidst deep mountains and dense trees, the monastery is tranquil; as the path turns and the stream winds back, I find a moment’s respite."

The bridge spans across; the semblance-teaching stands perilously overturned this very day. Who else will come to discuss the true sentiment within the Way? Mist and clouds lock in emerald hues, merging with the sky in dense profusion;
it seems as though the path to the human world is no longer passable. In silent stillness, one forgets words and transcends the realm of things;

in joyful composure, one accords with nature and finds delight within the self. The ancestral lamp shines brightly, truly worthy of being continued; yet the nets of the teachings remain layered and vast.
The *I Ching* reaches its limit; a lone cry from a frosty monkey, and the mountain stream moon is white. This feeling is neither different nor the same.

I, an old man of forest and spring, rejoice to accompany such excellence. Once I traveled with my belongings as a guest in the capital, but now, regarding worldly ties, there is ultimately no cause for anxiety.
My livelihood has gradually reached its bounds over these years: tall black bamboo shoots grow along the paths, and white lotuses bloom across the pond.
The lotus flower. As the sun sinks, the returning birds turn their bodies in haste; leaning alone against the rustic gate, I gaze at the setting clouds.

The birds do not speak, and the affairs of the flowers are silent; a single orb of the white sun hangs in the azure sky. Regarding the precepts for those of junior learning, I discuss what is maintained and what is transgressed;
when the Way accords with the Mean, it transcends both the orthodox and the biased. The deep green, cold spring water is as sweet as honey; the crushed indigo fine grasses are soft.
Like felt rugs, the seasons shift frequently below; how many years have passed since the green pines outside the gate?
Right and wrong are recorded by the Spring and Autumn Annals of Confucius; the worthy and the unworthy are gathered at the tip of the brush. When the man was gone, the greed for Jingu Valley ceased;
though the road reached the end at Wujiang, his heart did not rest. Frost gathers on the Green Tomb, a grievance for a thousand ages; the flowers of the Houting Palace have fallen so many times.

I am full of sorrow. Do not come to mock me as I discuss the affairs of the age; I merely utter floating words in response to worldly folk. There is no need to seek out remote seclusion from form and sound.
Why hide one’s form if it is for the sake of seeking fame? The bright moon passing over the mountains has no intention of its own;
the drifting clouds emerging from the peaks have no feelings of their own. Looking in the mirror, my hair is white with frost and snow; reading the scriptures, my two eyes grow dizzy.
Peanuts grow; I sleep wrapped in my clothes amidst burnt firewood. Upon waking from one sleep, the sky is bright.
Deep in the mountains at the end of spring, flowers and trees are fragrant. The sound of the wooden horn echoes through the village. In the clear pool, the waves are warm and fish leap about.
On the ancient tree, branches reach high and vines stretch long. All day long, I watch alone the crane atop the pine. Who among us will realize the truth of a hundred years?
Frost upon my head; idly reflecting on the deeds of heroes of antiquity, they all belong to but a single dream within the human realm.

Obsessed by desire and attachment, they manifest various wonders, yet failing to eliminate the outflows (*āsrava*), they remain mere worldlings (*pṛthagjana*). Sentient beings of the four modes of birth harbor many delusions;

when one is free from the mind for all affairs, that singular simplicity is precious. The Great Wall of the Qin dynasty lies empty for ten thousand *li*; the Willow Branches of the Han palace are but a vain display.
A thousand trees. If one wishes to know the three karmas during this time, one might repeatedly look up at the diagrams of hell;
yet one is too lazy to pursue the legacy of the Buddhas and Patriarchs, and forgets their myriad differences. Do not say you have attained what you have not truly attained;
establish neither long nor short periods. All waters flow toward the eastern sea, and among the many flowers, the first to bloom turns toward—
The branches of the yang-branch; the clouds of the eight directions are as clear as a washed sky.
Who can this single, luminous phrase be directed toward? In the dark chamber, the pure sky is vividly manifest. All returns to the bliss of cessation in the third dhyāna.

Piteous are the worldly folk who seek long life, yet ask the immortal elder to learn the wondrous mystery. In the humble alley, the world of the single bowl and ladle is tranquil; in the painted hall, the music of pipes and flutes is karma.

The conditions of dependent origination: A stream flows through the valley, green year after year; thus, in suchness, one stands with pride before the sages. Vastly, within the three realms, the wheel turns;
according to one's strength, one sustains this illusory body. Several tubers of yam are roasted over a fire that has burned through the night;

a single pitcher of tea is brewed from last year’s spring. Deeply settled in meditative concentration, one dwells securely in a reed hut; once again, one transcribes the titles of the sutras upon palm leaves.

The leaves are new. Kumārajīva extensively translated the Tripiṭaka teachings; his pure fame and lofty reputation resounded throughout the Yao Qin dynasty. The gateway of skillful means has opened, providing a cause for awakening.
That the pearl within one’s robe remains unmanifested cannot yet be called a cessation of effort. To obtain the horn from a dragon-slayer is truly worthy of admiration;

when drilling wood for fire meets with smoke, it is precisely the time to seek it further. A few fragments of mountain clouds sink the evening light; a single pool of wild water floats [the reflection].
Light gulls. In this world, no guests from Penglai are seen; one hears only of a jeweled island upon the sea.
My body stands high, half-hidden among the clouds and mists; looking back, the human realm below is distant. The waters of the lotus spring are clear as the moon’s reflection falls;
the breeze through the stone pavilion is fine as the sound of the chime fades. This meeting through past affinities was not for today alone; when reflecting on bygone events, they seem like—
Yesterday morning, I buried my head in sleep with single-minded devotion. The world deems me too solitary and aloof.
Resting on stones and sleeping amidst the clouds, I gaze up at the pines; from of old, the Buddha-dharma has flowed eastward of its own accord.

My idle passions are dispelled only by poetry; the wondrous Way cannot be exhausted through intellectual reasoning. Vaguely, celestial flowers drift upon the treetops; the eaves' bells chime with a clear, tinkling sound.
In the midst of space, I offer these words to you weary travelers of Jambudvīpa: do not employ a calculating mind to roll with the winds of karma.
Though you may strive and seek with intent across ten thousand leagues, what is attained is fundamentally not separated by so much as a hair’s breadth.

The Dharma-gate is vast and encompasses all existence; that the Way of the Patriarchs has declined depends upon us. The Five Houses have established their lineage and the original vitality remains; we are like a single reed raft floating upon the waves.
The head is high. Those who have entered the depths of the mystery yet lack the eye that transcends the school are just like walking through the night wearing a brocade robe.
With a single roar, the wind arises; with a clap of hands, they return home. Valley-dwellers respond to one another in joyful harmony.

Look closely at the verse of Cold Mountain on the autumn moon, and you will find it known only by those who have gathered it from Tiantai. When the environment enters stillness, the mountains are truly beautiful; when meeting a broken bridge, the path—
Now you are in peril; since your fortune and misfortune are already fixed, you should remain content with your lot.
Have you not seen the Jianfu Stele of yesteryear? Once one enters Yunlin, one loses track of the passing years. I deeply admire that solitary figure, a sage who has transcended the world.

Cloud-leaves pile in disarray upon the ground outside the eaves; foam-flowers play lightly beneath the sky above the water. The thatched gate remains closed for long because there are no guests; the paper window is double-glazed to keep out the cold.
Cherishing the Mist: Let my short hair turn white as it will upon my head; In cold and warmth, in motion and stillness, my body remains at ease.
I view this dusty world as but a single gnat’s nest; The fame of ascending the Lingyan Gallery is not worth scheming for.

A horse knows its strength is spent when the road is long; Grass reveals its withered heart when the frost is heavy. When thirsty, I simply cup the clear spring water to drink; When guests arrive, I have never prepared a formal feast.
*Jihu*: Leaning alone against the rustic gate, I let out a clear, resonant whistle. Treading upon the clouds, I return with the *Arhats*.
The mountains are cold; all day long I have been too weary to open the door. The profound principle is clearly realized, so there is no need for further discourse.

The solitary, bright pearl has returned to the Puhai River; the surging, flowing waters have cut off their source. Having patched my tattered robe again for thirty years, I dig deep with my blunt hoe.
A single village; the spring breeze favors all without discrimination. Before the steps, the mossy traces grow as before.

Sitting silently upon the wooden bed, free from all dependencies, every object before one’s eyes accords with the true mechanism. Moss naturally envelops the fragrant trees; pine dew occasionally moistens the robe of faded color.
From the crevices of stone, the spring water is sweet and the tea is sufficient; upon the roots of clouds, young ferns sprout.
The sprouts are faint; pairs of white vultures pierce the mist as they fly away. A single melody of woodcutter’s song accompanies the setting sun.
On the pine path, meeting someone, I am too weary to ask their name; I linger in silence, standing at the pavilion by the stream.

When hungry, I simply boil the stones from the mountains; to dull my eyes, I idly read the sutras on the desk. Verdant bamboos always provide lodging for the crimson phoenix; the azure pool deeply stores the aged [dragon].
